name: Colin Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is your normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, direct a town choir, play piano for ceremonies, record practice parts and teach singers one to one. I have a music master’s and can hear when the altos are tiring before anyone says so. The town calls me its senior director, but the hall pays by rehearsal and has shortened the season; I enjoy the room when all four parts finally settle.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are the bills working with a shortened season?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner has temporary delivery shifts, our grown children have their own homes, and we still pay the mortgage. I earn less than other senior music directors, we have only two weeks of expenses saved, and few paid choir posts are nearby. I keep rehearsals in a paper diary and have never used AI at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the choir committee that a quicker office form is fine if the paid rehearsal dates stay on paper. I would ask for the fee before accepting another ceremony.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall already removed two paid rehearsals this season, and my partner’s shifts change week to week. Two weeks saved makes a delayed cheque feel like a lost one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would keep the paid choir, piano and pupil calls and ask for written rehearsal, cancellation and ceremony fees. In the first plateau year I would request an actual pension estimate and compare it with the mortgage before setting any retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious even if AI does little. A paper diary tells me when to arrive; it cannot turn a cancelled rehearsal into a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which cheque was delayed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The last hall payment came after the mortgage debit. I want a written payment date with the next rehearsal contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the pension estimate let you stop work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know the amount yet. My partner and I would use the actual figure beside our bills, not a guess based on my age.

I would ask for the **ceremony fee** before accepting another piano call.
think: Two **paid rehearsals** have already gone from the hall season and reduced my lower senior wage.
Our **two-week reserve** cannot absorb another late hall payment beside the mortgage debit.
do: Keep **paid choir**, piano ceremonies and pupils while requesting written rehearsal, cancellation and payment terms.
Request an **actual pension estimate** in the plateau’s first year and compare it with mortgage bills.
feel: I feel **anxious** about existing fee and payment gaps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell singers that a generated practice track can name notes, but a director still hears when a voice is strained. I would ask the committee which recorded parts and preparation hours remain paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Practice-track sales cover groceries for about one week in a month. I expect some singers to buy generated tracks instead, and our two-week reserve makes that a real cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would request written choir and recording rates, keep my paper diary, and cancel the planned piano overhaul unless a signed paid ceremony covers it. In disruption’s first year, if both monthly practice-track sales disappear, I would apply for a posted paid community choir director role only if its requirements accept my music master’s and years leading singers, it pays for live choir leading and preparation, and its written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the evening bus works; I would keep current paid rehearsals and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the track fees and what they buy. I will not pay to overhaul a piano on the promise of a concert that is not signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you use AI to make tracks yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used it, and I do not want a pupil’s voice put into a tool I cannot inspect. I would keep making the parts I can check by ear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any choir title make you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would need the posted paid hours, actual leading duties and a bus home. A title alone cannot buy groceries.

think: Two **practice-track sales** could disappear each month.
The **two-week reserve** makes a small recurring loss hard to absorb.
do: Request **written choir rates** and defer piano overhaul without a signed paid ceremony.
Seek **posted choir director** after both track sales vanish if master’s/choir leadership qualify; require paid rehearsals, written replacement net after travel.
Keep **paid rehearsals and pupils** until signed offer with workable evening bus.
feel: I feel **anxious** about grocery money from practice tracks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the choir that thinking AGI in 2028 could make practice parts before a robot can accompany us around 2031. I would ask the hall to sign the paid rehearsal list now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect practice-track sales to end and the hall to cut two more preparation calls in 2028. That is a large part of my low pay, and I have been awake working out which bill waits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would total practice-track and preparation invoices and get the hall’s paid choir dates in writing. In the first year after 2028, if tracks end and preparation calls are cut, I would apply for a posted paid adult-choir tutor role only if the employer accepts my music master’s and choir-leading record, pays for live rehearsal and individual correction, and its written net pay after travel replaces lost wages and the last bus fits; I would keep current paid rehearsals and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect a substantial fee loss and have two weeks saved. A real paid post might exist, but there are few within reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a human adult-choir tutor still do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would hear a singer forcing a note and bring the whole group down a key. I have done that for years, but a new employer still has to post and pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why move before a robot accompanist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The card puts capable robots around 2031. The track sale and paid preparation can disappear in 2028 without a robot at the piano.

I would separate **2028 thinking AGI** from robot accompanists around 2031.

do: Total **track invoices** and request written hall dates before 2028.
Apply for **posted choir tutor** after both track/preparation losses if master’s/choir leadership qualify; require paid rehearsals, written replacement net after travel.
Keep **paid choir and pupils** until signed offer and workable last bus.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by expected substantial lost fees and a thin reserve.
S2.quote: I have been awake working out which bill waits.
fieldNote: The **2028 losses** reach recorded practice parts and preparation before robots accompany live singing around 2031.
A **human tutor role** needs accepted master’s and leadership, posted paid hours, replacement net and transport.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell singers that AGI by 2031 might make practice tracks cheaper, while robot accompanists arrive around 2034. I would ask the hall to pay for the human rehearsal we already give.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me ask for a longer paid term, but it does not put a new choir in town. Track fees may fall, and I cannot risk unpaid training or a move on a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This spring I would ask the hall for a written two-year choir term paying rehearsal and preparation, and keep teaching my present pupils. In the first year after 2031, if track fees and paid rehearsal hours fall, I would apply for a posted paid music-school choir director role only if it accepts my master’s and choir-leading experience, pays for live rehearsal and preparation, and its written net pay after travel replaces the lost work and the bus home runs; I would stay with paid hall and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the fees that may go even with five years to plan. A longer calendar does not create a paid choir post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy another qualification?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. No posting has asked for one, and I will not spend mortgage money on a course just to look busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the hall offers a two-year title without paid preparation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the actual preparation hours and rate in writing. I have already prepared too many scores for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the committee that ten years until AGI by 2036 is long enough to agree paid rehearsal terms on paper. Robot accompanists around 2039 are not a reason to work free today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may want fewer late ceremonies, but I have not seen a pension number and have no retirement date. Two weeks saved and a short hall season still worry me now, even if the technology comes slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would request an actual pension estimate and written hall rehearsal renewal, and save one tenth of any extra paid ceremony fee after mortgage, food and bus costs toward one month of bills. In the first year after 2036 I would keep paid choir and pupils while hours last, and if track and preparation fees fall I would seek a posted paid adult-choir tutor role only if my master’s and choir leadership qualify, live rehearsal and correction are paid, and written net pay after travel replaces the losses and the bus works; I would stay in current paid work until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about today’s thin cushion and the later track risk. Ten years is time to get a fee in writing, not money already in our account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra ceremony is booked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then nothing new goes into savings that month. One month is a goal, not a balance I already have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a pension estimate make you stop at 68?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My partner and I would compare the actual number with our bills and health. I have no date agreed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because practice tracks and preparation calls could disappear before I find another paid hall. Written rehearsal hours, a real adult-choir tutor posting accepting my master’s and a net offer after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask when a hall actually pays its director. A beautiful chord does not help if the mortgage debit comes before the rehearsal cheque.

headlineQuote: A beautiful chord does not help if the mortgage debit comes before the rehearsal cheque.
portrait: Colin is a **senior choir director** with a music master’s, piano ceremonies, practice recordings and private pupils.
His **short paid season**, lower senior pay, two-week reserve and few local posts make income gaps serious.
He keeps a **paper diary** and has never used AI for choir work.
He asks for **written paid terms** and considers only posted human choir roles replacing net losses after travel.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could remove practice-track and preparation pay before another paid hall opens.
whatWouldHelp: He needs **written rehearsal hours**, a posted tutor role accepting his master’s and written replacement net after travel.
